Impact

What We Lose When a Tradition Fades

Behind every craft are real people, real places and real stories. Here is what is at stake.

The issue in numbers

India's handloom sector is one of the biggest sources of traditional craft work. These figures come from the Government of India's Fourth All India Handloom Census (2019–20).

  • 35.22 lakh

    handloom weavers and allied workers in India (about 3.5 million people).

    Source: Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20, Ministry of Textiles, as reported by PIB (2026).

  • 72%

    of handloom workers are women: about 25.46 lakh people.

    Source: Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20, as reported by PIB (2026).

  • 66.3%

    of weaver households earn less than ₹5,000 a month.

    Source: Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20, summary in the PARI Library.

  • 31.45 lakh

    households in India are engaged in handloom work.

    Source: Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20, as reported by PIB (2026).

Six ways the loss is felt

  1. 01

    People

    Artisans lose work and income, and their years of skill go unused.

  2. 02

    Communities

    Villages built around a craft can lose jobs, markets and pride.

  3. 03

    Traditions

    Techniques that took centuries to develop can vanish in one generation.

  4. 04

    Identity

    Crafts, songs and dances help people know where they come from.

  5. 05

    Language

    Each craft has its own words for tools and steps. When a craft stops, those words are used less.

  6. 06

    Culture

    Festivals, food and art lose some of the colour that makes them special.

Real places, real crafts

  • Bagru block printing

    Rajasthan. Hand-printed cloth with natural dyes. Learn about Bagru printing

  • Pedana Kalamkari

    Andhra Pradesh. Block-printed cloth coloured with plant dyes. Learn about Kalamkari

  • Dindigul lock-making

    Tamil Nadu. Handmade metal locks made by skilled lock-smiths. (Image: general metal-craft illustration.)

Traditions can recover

The story is not only about loss. In 2019, Dindigul locks were registered as a Geographical Indication (GI). A GI tag means only locks made in that area, in the traditional way, can use the name. It protects the craft and helps buyers find the real thing.

India also marks National Handloom Day on 7 August every year since 2015, to honour weavers and their work.

Sources: IP India GI Registry, Dindigul Locks; MyGov, National Handloom Day.

Sources

  • Ministry of Textiles, Office of the Development Commissioner (Handlooms). Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20. Figures as reported in a Press Information Bureau document (August 2026).
  • PARI Library summary of the Fourth All India Handloom Census 2019–20.
  • IP India, Geographical Indications Registry: Dindigul Locks.
  • MyGov, National Handloom Day.
